<STRUCT_0001>
It is not completely clear that the small Zariski site,
the big affine Zariski site, and the small affine Zariski site
are sites. We check this now.

Let <MATH_0001> be a scheme. Let <MATH_0002> be a big Zariski
site containing <MATH_0003>. The structures <MATH_0004>, <MATH_0005>,
and <MATH_0006> defined above are sites.

Let us show that <MATH_0001> is a site. It is a category with a
given set of families of morphisms with fixed target. Thus we
have to show properties (1), (2) and (3) of
Sites, Definition <REF_0001>.
Since <MATH_0002> is a site, it suffices to prove
that given any covering <MATH_0003> of <MATH_0004>
with <MATH_0005> we also have <MATH_0006>.
This follows from the definitions
as the composition of open immersions is an open immersion.

<STRUCT_0001><STRUCT_0002>
Let us show that <MATH_0007> is a site.
Reasoning as above, it suffices to show that the collection
of standard Zariski coverings of affines satisfies properties
(1), (2) and (3) of
Sites, Definition <REF_0002>.
Let <MATH_0008> be a ring. Let <MATH_0009> generate the unit ideal.
For each <MATH_0010> let <MATH_0011>
be elements generating the unit ideal of <MATH_0012>. Write
<MATH_0013> which is possible. After replacing
<MATH_0014> by <MATH_0015> if necessary, we have that
<MATH_0016> is
equal to <MATH_0017>. Hence we see that
the family of morphisms <MATH_0018>
is a standard Zariski covering. From these considerations
it follows that (2) holds for standard Zariski coverings.
We omit the verification of (1) and (3).

We omit the proof that <MATH_0019> is a site.
